youtube.title: The Most Famous Loch Ness Monster Photo Was a Toy Submarine
youtube.description:
In 1934, a London newspaper published a photograph of a long neck and small head rising from Loch Ness, credited to London doctor R. Kenneth Wilson: the "Surgeon's Photograph." For about sixty years it was considered the best evidence for the Loch Ness Monster. Months earlier, big-game hunter Marmaduke Wetherell had been ridiculed after "monster" footprints he found turned out to be made with a hippo's foot. In 1994, his stepson Christian Spurling, then in his nineties, confessed that he had built the monster from a sculpted head and neck attached to a toy submarine, and that the doctor was the trusted name used to sell the picture.

📂 Case File #035: The Surgeon's Photograph

Sources: Museum of Hoaxes, "The Loch Ness Monster and the Surgeon's Photo"; PBS NOVA, "The Beast of Loch Ness".
Images (Wikimedia Commons): Surgeon's Photograph, 1934 (public domain); Loch Ness and Urquhart Castle (CC BY 3.0); misty Loch Ness (CC BY-SA 2.0).
